section.title: The Conquest of Bashan
section.sectionRationale: This closes Moses' historical review of the wilderness journey with the second great Transjordan victory, over Og of Bashan, the allotment of that land, and Moses' own poignant, personal exclusion from the land he has led Israel toward for forty years.
section.thesis: As Israel completes the conquest of the Transjordan by defeating Og, the last of the giant kings, Moses allots that land to two and a half tribes on condition that they first help their brothers conquer the land west of the Jordan, then pleads with the LORD to cross over himself and is refused, though he is granted a view of the land and commissions Joshua as his successor.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the defeat of Og king of Bashan; the land taken and divided; instructions to the two and a half tribes; Moses commissions Joshua; and Moses' plea, met by the LORD's firm but merciful refusal.

units.label: The defeat of Og king of Bashan

verses.text: Then we turned and went up the road to Bashan, and Og king of Bashan and his whole army came out to meet us in battle at Edrei.
But the LORD said to me, “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon.”
So the LORD our God also delivered Og king of Bashan and his whole army into our hands. We struck them down until no survivor was left.
At that time we captured all sixty of his cities. There was not a single city we failed to take, the entire region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.
All these cities were fortified with high walls and gates and bars, and there were many more unwalled villages.
We devoted them to destruction, as we had done to Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men, women, and children of every city.
But all the livestock and plunder of the cities we carried off for ourselves.
At that time we took from the two kings of the Amorites the land across the Jordan, from the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Hermon,
which the Sidonians call Sirion but the Amorites call Senir,
all the cities of the plateau, all of Gilead, and all of Bashan as far as the cities of Salecah and Edrei in the kingdom of Og.
(For only Og king of Bashan had remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. His bed of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide, is still in Rabbah of the Ammonites.)
So at that time we took possession of this land. To the Reubenites and Gadites I gave the land beyond Aroer along the Arnon Valley, and half the hill country of Gilead, along with its cities.
To the half-tribe of Manasseh I gave the rest of Gilead and all of Bashan, the kingdom of Og. (The entire region of Argob, the whole territory of Bashan, used to be called the land of the Rephaim.)

Jair, a descendant of Manasseh, took the whole region of Argob as far as the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites. He renamed Bashan after himself, Havvoth-jair, by which it is called to this day.
To Machir I gave Gilead,
and to the Reubenites and Gadites I gave the territory from Gilead to the Arnon Valley (the middle of the valley was the border) and up to the Jabbok River, the border of the Ammonites.
The Jordan River in the Arabah bordered it from Chinnereth to the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea) with the slopes of Pisgah to the east.

units.label: Instructions to the two and a half tribes

verses.text: At that time I commanded you: “The LORD your God has given you this land to possess. All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites.
But your wives, your children, and your livestock, I know that you have much livestock, may remain in the cities I have given you,

until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you, and they too have taken possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them across the Jordan. Then each of you may return to the {{nachalah|possession}} I have given you.”

units.label: Moses commissions Joshua
units.note: the LORD Himself will fight for you

verses.text: And at that time I commanded Joshua: “Your own eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings. The LORD will do the same to all the kingdoms you are about to enter.
Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you.”

units.label: Moses' plea, and the LORD's refusal
units.note: enough, do not speak to Me again

verses.text: At that time I also {{chanan|pleaded}} with the LORD:
“O Lord GOD, You have begun to show Your greatness and power to Your servant. For what god in heaven or on earth can perform such works and mighty acts as Yours?
Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan, that pleasant hill country as well as Lebanon!”
But the LORD was angry with me on account of you, and He would not listen to me. “That is enough,” the LORD said to me. “Do not speak to Me again about this matter.
Go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west and north and south and east. See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan.
But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him, for he will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit the land that you will see.”
So we stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor.

chanan.gloss: To seek favor, to plead earnestly for grace; the root behind the Hebrew word for grace, chen. Moses does not demand entry to the land as a right but pleads for it as an undeserved favor, and even this plea is refused.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, allotted possession. Used of the land given to each tribe, it points to land as a gift held in trust from the LORD rather than property earned or seized by human effort alone.

basic.context: Moses finishes the Transjordan conquest narrative with the defeat of Og, the giant king of Bashan, the division of that land among two and a half tribes, and his own deeply personal plea to enter the promised land, which the LORD firmly refuses even as He shows Moses mercy in other ways.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history retold with theological weight: the defeat of a legendary giant-king shows the LORD's power, while Moses' refused request shows that even history's greatest servant of God does not escape the consequences of his own sin, yet is still treated with tenderness by God.
basic.originalLanguages: Moses says he chanan, pleaded or sought favor, with the LORD, using the very word behind chen, grace, showing he asked for an undeserved gift rather than a right owed him. The land given to the tribes is their nachalah, inheritance, a gift held in trust from God rather than territory simply seized by conquest.
basic.typology: Moses, the great mediator who leads Israel to the very border of the land but cannot enter it himself, anticipates the need for a greater mediator who both leads His people fully into their inheritance and shares fully in it with them, fulfilled in Jesus, the true and greater Joshua.
basic.christ: Moses' exclusion from the land, despite his faithful service, points to the insufficiency of even the greatest human mediator; Hebrews 3:1-6 contrasts Moses as a faithful servant in God's house with Christ as the faithful Son who builds and inherits the house itself.
basic.god: God is powerful enough to defeat a legendary giant-king in a single battle, yet He is also firm and personal enough to say no to His most faithful servant's heartfelt plea, while still showing Moses real kindness by letting him see the land and by entrusting Joshua to his personal encouragement.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 21:33-35 gives the parallel account of Og's defeat. Hebrews 3:1-6 contrasts Moses the servant with Christ the Son. Deuteronomy 34:1-4 records Moses actually viewing the land from Pisgah as promised here.
basic.oneStory: The God who defeats giants and apportions inheritances is the same God who lovingly, firmly says no to His faithful servant Moses, revealing that even the greatest human leader cannot bring God's people fully into their rest. That work waits for a greater mediator, Jesus, who leads His people all the way home.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 completes the historical retrospect that began in 1:6, and it is built to be read beside the Sihon account of 2:24-37. The Og narrative follows the same sequence almost word for word: the enemy comes out to battle, God says 'Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand,' verse 2, the cities are taken, the people are devoted to destruction, and the livestock and plunder are kept, verses 6 and 7. God Himself draws the parallel: 'Do to him as you did to Sihon,' verse 2. Two kings, one pattern, and from here on 'Sihon and Og' become a single memory.

The chapter is marked off by the repeated phrase 'at that time,' verses 4, 8, 12, 18, 21 and 23. Each occurrence opens a new movement: the capture of the cities, the extent of the conquered land, its allotment, the charge to the eastern tribes, the charge to Joshua, and Moses' prayer. The effect is of a leader looking back over a crowded season and gathering it into a sequence of scenes.

Parenthetical notes again interrupt the narrative: the two other names for Hermon, verse 9, Og's iron bed, verse 11, the old name 'land of the Rephaim,' verse 13, and the naming of Havvoth-jair, verse 14. As in chapter 2 they speak to later hearers, 'to this day.'

The last scene turns from public history to private prayer. Moses' plea, verses 23 to 25, and God's refusal, verses 26 to 28, mirror the charge to Joshua just before. Joshua is told, 'Your own eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done,' verse 21; Moses is told, 'See the land with your own eyes,' verse 27. Joshua's eyes look back on victories he will repeat; Moses' eyes look forward to a land he will not enter. The chapter then ends quietly, 'we stayed in the valley opposite Beth-peor,' verse 29, the place where Moses will be buried, Deuteronomy 34:6, and the scene of the sin that chapter 4 recalls, 4:3.
context.historical:
Bashan was the high, well watered plateau east of the Sea of Galilee, running north toward Mount Hermon. Its volcanic soil made it famous for cattle and timber. The prophets speak of the 'cows of Bashan,' Amos 4:1, the 'strong bulls of Bashan,' Psalm 22:12, and the 'oaks of Bashan,' Isaiah 2:13. Og ruled from Ashtaroth and fought at Edrei, 1:4 and 3:1, both on the southern edge of the plateau. Joshua 12:4 calls him 'one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei.'

The region of Argob with its sixty cities, verse 4, was still remembered in Solomon's day as 'the region of Argob in Bashan with its sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars,' 1 Kings 4:13. Verse 5 notes that besides the walled towns there were 'many more unwalled villages,' a picture of a dense, prosperous kingdom rather than a scattered frontier.

Og's bed of iron, verse 11, measured nine cubits by four, which the BSB footnote gives as about fourteen feet by six. In the Late Bronze Age iron was a costly, prestigious material, so an iron bed was a royal object as much as a large one. Some interpreters have suggested the Hebrew word could describe a basalt sarcophagus, since the dark basalt of Bashan resembles iron; the text itself simply calls it a bed. It was kept in Rabbah of the Ammonites, perhaps as a trophy or relic, where later hearers could still see it.

The allotment follows Numbers 32. Reuben and Gad asked for the Transjordan because they had 'much livestock,' Numbers 32:1, and Moses agreed only on condition that their soldiers cross with the other tribes, Numbers 32:20-22. Machir and Jair, clans of Manasseh, had taken Gilead and its villages, Numbers 32:39-41. Pisgah, verse 27, is the headland of the Abarim range overlooking the Jordan valley near Mount Nebo, Deuteronomy 34:1, from which on a clear day much of the land to the west can be seen.
context.canonical:
The defeat of Og is first told in Numbers 21:33-35, whose wording Deuteronomy 3:1-3 closely follows. Joshua 12:1-6 lists Sihon and Og at the head of the kings Israel defeated, and Joshua 13:8-32 describes the allotment of their lands in detail. Rahab, the Gibeonites, the psalmists and the Levites of Nehemiah's day all name the two kings together, Joshua 2:10, Joshua 9:10, Psalm 135:11, Psalm 136:19-20 and Nehemiah 9:22. Amos 2:9 recalls the Amorite whose 'height was like that of the cedars,' and says God destroyed him.

The Rephaim do not disappear with Og. Descendants of Rapha in Gath fell 'at the hands of David and his servants,' 2 Samuel 21:22, and Goliath of Gath stood 'six cubits and a span,' 1 Samuel 17:4. The victory over Og is the first of a series in which the LORD's people bring down the giants that frightened the Kadesh generation.

The condition laid on the eastern tribes, verses 18 to 20, is traced through Joshua. Joshua reminds them of it, Joshua 1:12-15, they cross armed, Joshua 4:12, and they are sent home with praise, 'you have not deserted your brothers,' Joshua 22:3. Yet their location proved vulnerable: they were the first carried into exile by Tiglath-pileser, 1 Chronicles 5:26.

Moses' exclusion runs through the rest of the Pentateuch: Numbers 27:12-14, Deuteronomy 31:2, 32:48-52 and 34:1-5. The commissioning of Joshua is fulfilled in Numbers 27:18-23, Deuteronomy 31:7-8 and 23, and Joshua 1:1-9. The New Testament brings Moses into the land at last, speaking with Jesus on the mountain of transfiguration about 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:30-31. Hebrews 3:1-6 sets Moses the servant beside Christ the Son, and Paul's thrice repeated plea in 2 Corinthians 12:8-9 is answered in a way that echoes Moses' own refusal.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses tells the story of Og to finish a lesson begun at Kadesh. The Kadesh generation had said, 'We even saw the descendants of the Anakim there,' 1:28. Now Moses tells their children that Og, 'the remnant of the Rephaim,' verse 11, fell with all sixty of his fortified cities. The pointed detail of the bed of iron lets the hearers measure the enemy and then measure the God who defeated him. The lesson is stated directly to Joshua: 'The LORD will do the same to all the kingdoms you are about to enter,' verse 21.

He records the allotment to the eastern tribes so that the whole nation will remember a promise. The men of Reuben, Gad and Manasseh must not settle into their rest while their brothers still fight, verses 18 to 20. The unity of Israel is at stake, and Moses wants it written into the story.

Finally, he tells his own story with remarkable honesty. He pleaded and was refused. He does not hide that God was angry with him, verse 26, or that the answer was final. He wants Israel to understand that he will not lead them over, that Joshua must, and that their obedience cannot hang on his presence. His own disappointment becomes part of his preaching: God is holy, His word stands, and the people's future lies with the leader God has appointed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nearly everything in this chapter is description: a battle, a land division, a commission and a private conversation between Moses and God. None of it is a command for later readers to repeat. Believers are not told to take land, devote cities or divide territories.

Some elements model patterns that Scripture elsewhere commends. The eastern tribes' obligation to fight for their brothers before enjoying their own rest illustrates the solidarity that the New Testament asks of the church, 'Carry one another's burdens,' Galatians 6:2. Moses' charge to 'encourage him, and strengthen him,' verse 28, models the work of preparing the next generation of leaders.

Moses' prayer must be read with care. It shows that it is right to bring earnest requests to God and to plead on the basis of His greatness rather than our merit, verse 24. It also shows that God may say no, even to His faithful servants, and that His no is not the end of His kindness. The passage does not teach that every unanswered prayer is a sign of divine anger; it records a particular judgment on a particular sin, Numbers 20:12. The abiding lesson is submission, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39.

debates.question: Was God's refusal of Moses' plea harsh or merciful?

views.label: It appears severe given Moses' lifetime of service
views.case: Moses had led Israel faithfully for forty years through immense hardship, and his failure at Meribah seems small compared with the people's repeated rebellions. The abrupt 'That is enough. Do not speak to Me again about this matter,' verse 26, can feel disproportionate.

views.label: It is a serious but merciful judgment
views.case: God lets Moses see the whole land from Pisgah, verse 27, entrusts him with commissioning Joshua, verse 28, and buries him Himself, Deuteronomy 34:6. The New Testament shows Moses at last speaking with Christ in glory, Luke 9:30-31. The consequence is real, but it is surrounded by tenderness.

views.label: The refusal protects the holiness God's servant failed to honour
views.case: Numbers 20:12 names the sin as failing 'to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites.' A leader who misrepresents God publicly bears a public consequence, as James 3:1 says of teachers. On this view the severity is exactly in proportion to the visibility of Moses' office.

debates.bearing: The views are not mutually exclusive. God's refusal is holy, because Moses' sin was public, and it is kind, because it comes with a view of the land, a meaningful task, a burial by God's own hand and a later place beside Christ in glory.

debates.question: Was the land east of the Jordan part of the promised land?

views.label: Yes, it was a genuine gift of God
views.case: Moses says 'The LORD your God has given you this land to possess,' verse 18, and uses the language of rest for the eastern tribes, verse 20. The original promise reached 'as far as the great River Euphrates,' 1:7, which would include the Transjordan. Joshua 13 allots it as the tribes' inheritance.

views.label: It had a secondary, ambiguous status
views.case: The boundary list in Numbers 34:12 makes the Jordan the eastern border of Canaan, and Moses was initially angry at the request, Numbers 32:6-15. In Joshua 22:19 the western tribes say, 'If indeed the land of your inheritance is unclean, then cross over to the land of the LORD's possession.' The eastern tribes had to build a memorial altar to prove they belonged, Joshua 22:24-28.

debates.bearing: Deuteronomy treats the Transjordan as a true gift, while other texts show that its separation by the river created ongoing questions of identity. The practical lesson of Deuteronomy 3 is that a gift received early must not separate one part of God's people from the rest.

study.originalLanguages:
Og is 'the remnant of the Rephaim,' verse 11, and the region of Argob 'used to be called the land of the Rephaim,' verse 13. The name is used in Deuteronomy for an ancient race of tall peoples, 2:11 and 2:20. Elsewhere the same word refers to the shades of the dead in the underworld: 'Do departed spirits rise up to praise You?' Psalm 88:10, and 'The dead will not live; the departed spirits will not rise,' Isaiah 26:14. The connection between the two uses is debated and should not be pressed, but for a Hebrew reader the name carried an air of the ancient and the ominous. The last of that race falls in a single campaign.

Moses addresses God as 'O Lord GOD,' verse 24. The BSB prints GOD in capitals where the Hebrew divine name stands after Adonai, 'Lord' or 'Master,' so the phrase joins the language of a servant to his master with the covenant name. He calls himself 'Your servant,' and Deuteronomy's last chapter gives him the same title, 'Moses the servant of the LORD,' Deuteronomy 34:5. He uses the same address in his great intercession after the golden calf, Deuteronomy 9:26. His plea to enter the land comes from the posture of a servant, not a partner with rights.

In the same verse Moses praises God's 'greatness,' godel. The word gathers up the exodus and conquest: 'the LORD our God has shown us His glory and greatness,' Deuteronomy 5:24; 'His greatness, His mighty hand,' 11:2; and Moses' own song, 'Ascribe greatness to our God!' 32:3. Moses' question, 'what god in heaven or on earth can perform such works,' echoes the Song of the Sea, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?' Exodus 15:11.

The story of the refusal turns on a pun. Moses asks, 'Please let me cross over,' verse 25, using avar, to cross. The next verse says 'the LORD was angry with me,' and the verb there is the reflexive form of the same root, used for anger that overflows its bounds. God tells him in verse 27, 'you will not cross this Jordan.' The man who wanted to cross over meets a God whose anger crossed over against him. English cannot keep the play, but it binds the prayer and the answer together.

God's reply opens with 'That is enough,' rav lakh. It is the phrase with which God began the whole journey, 'You have stayed at this mountain long enough,' 1:6, and with which He ended the wandering, 2:3. Korah used it against Moses, 'You have taken too much upon yourselves!' Numbers 16:3, and Moses threw it back in 16:7. Now it is turned on Moses himself. The word that released Israel from delay closes Moses' appeal.

Finally, God commands Moses to 'encourage him, and strengthen him,' verse 28, from chazaq and amats. These two verbs become the refrain of the handover: 'Be strong and courageous,' Deuteronomy 31:7 and 31:23, Joshua 1:6-7. The second verb has already appeared in the story. When God made Sihon's heart 'obstinate,' 2:30, the verb was amats. The same strengthening of heart can harden a king against God or steady a servant for God's work.

typology.type: Moses, the faithful mediator who cannot enter
typology.fulfillment: Moses led Israel out of Egypt, through the wilderness and to the border, but not into the land. Hebrews 3:5-6 names the difference: Moses 'was faithful as a servant in all God's house,' but 'Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house.' Moses was barred because of his own sin; Christ, 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, not only enters but opens the way for His people. The type shows the need; the fulfilment supplies it. Where Moses' exclusion reminds Israel that even the greatest human mediator falls short, Christ's entry guarantees that His people will follow Him in.

typology.type: Og, the last of the Rephaim, overthrown
typology.fulfillment: The giant king whose bed was kept as a monument fell with all his sixty cities, and later generations remembered it as proof that no enemy is too great for the LORD. The line of giants reappears at Gath and falls to David and his servants, 2 Samuel 21:22. The New Testament points to a greater victory over a greater enemy, Christ disarming 'the powers and authorities,' Colossians 2:15, and destroying 'him who holds the power of death,' Hebrews 2:14. The type falls short because Og was flesh and blood, while the enemies Christ defeats are spiritual powers and death itself.

typology.type: Joshua commissioned to enable Israel to inherit
typology.fulfillment: Moses must 'commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him, for he will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit,' verse 28. Joshua goes ahead of the people and causes them to inherit. Hebrews calls Jesus the 'forerunner' who 'has entered on our behalf,' Hebrews 6:20, and the one who brings 'many sons to glory,' Hebrews 2:10. The type falls short because Joshua needed to be encouraged and strengthened by another, and his rest was not final, Hebrews 4:8. Christ is not a successor who needs another's encouragement but the Son sent by the Father, and the rest He gives is eternal.

typology.type: Moses viewing the land from Pisgah
typology.fulfillment: Moses was allowed to see what he could not yet possess. Hebrews 11:13 describes the patriarchs the same way: they 'died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar.' The picture of the servant on the mountain seeing the promise from a distance is fulfilled when Moses appears with Jesus in glory, Matthew 17:3, and in the promise that the faithful of old will be 'made perfect' together with the church, Hebrews 11:40. What Moses saw from Pisgah was a land; what he received in Christ was the inheritance the land pointed to.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the failure of the best human mediator. Moses is the prophet with whom God spoke face to face, and in this chapter he intercedes for himself, eloquently and humbly, and is refused. His exclusion is a sober reminder that the law, and the servant who gave it, could bring God's people to the edge of the promise but not into it. John 1:17 draws the line: 'the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.' Hebrews 3:1-6 makes the same comparison in terms of a servant and a son.

It leads to Christ through a prayer that was not granted. Moses pleaded, using the language of grace, and God said no. In Gethsemane the Son of God prayed, 'My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me,' Matthew 26:39, and the cup did not pass. Hebrews 5:7 says that He 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears,' and was heard. The difference is that Moses was refused because of his own sin, while Jesus drank the cup because of ours. His unanswered request became the means by which every other promise of God is answered, 2 Corinthians 1:20. Paul, pleading three times over his thorn, heard a reply that echoes Moses' 'That is enough': 'My grace is sufficient for you,' 2 Corinthians 12:9.

It leads to Christ through the transfiguration. Moses, who was told 'you will not cross this Jordan,' stands inside the land with Elijah and Jesus, Matthew 17:3, speaking of His 'departure,' the Greek word exodos, 'which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31. The refusal of Deuteronomy 3 was not God's last word to Moses. He enters in the company of the One who leads the greater exodus.

It leads to Christ through the victories. The God who told Joshua 'the LORD your God Himself will fight for you,' verse 22, fights for His people in Christ, who overcomes the strong man and plunders his house, Mark 3:27.

And it leads to Christ through the eastern tribes' promise to fight until their brothers have rest. Christ did not keep His rest to Himself. Though He shared the Father's glory, He came to fight for His brothers and sisters, and He is 'not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11. The image is an analogy rather than a declared type, but it captures the shape of His love.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the one who gives victory. The defeat of Og is described as God's act before it is Israel's: 'I have delivered him into your hand,' verse 2, and 'the LORD our God also delivered Og king of Bashan,' verse 3. The sixty fortified cities with 'high walls and gates and bars,' verse 5, fell because God gave them. Moses' own praise interprets the campaign: 'You have begun to show Your greatness and power to Your servant,' verse 24.

He is incomparable. 'What god in heaven or on earth can perform such works and mighty acts as Yours?' verse 24. Chapter 4 will develop this into the confession that 'the LORD is God; there is no other,' 4:35. The victory over the last of the Rephaim is not merely a military success; it is a revelation of who God is.

He is the owner and giver of the land. Moses says 'I gave' the territories, verses 12 to 16, but he also says 'the LORD your God has given you this land,' verse 18. Human distribution rests on divine gift. The eastern tribes receive their portion as a trust, which is why it comes with an obligation to their brothers.

He is holy, and His word stands even when His dearest servant asks Him to change it. God had sworn that Moses would not enter, and He would not listen, verse 26. The refusal shows that God's holiness is not softened by personal closeness. The prophet who knew Him face to face was still held to what God had said.

Yet He is also tender. He does not merely say no. He tells Moses to climb Pisgah and look in every direction, verse 27. He gives him a task, to encourage and strengthen Joshua, verse 28. And Deuteronomy 34:6 records that God Himself buried Moses. God's discipline of His servants is never merely punitive; it is the discipline of a father who does not cease to love.

He is the God who continues His work beyond any one servant. Moses must stop, but the story does not. Joshua 'will cross over ahead of the people,' verse 28. God's purposes are not tied to the lifespan of His instruments, which Moses himself celebrates in the prayer the Psalter attributes to him: 'Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations,' Psalm 90:1.

For worship, the chapter invites us to praise God's greatness for past victories, to bring Him our requests as servants rather than claimants, and to trust Him when He says no.

crossReferences.note: Numbers tells the battle at Edrei in words that Deuteronomy 3:1-3 repeats, including God's reassurance, 'Do not fear him,' and the instruction to do to Og as to Sihon. Moses' retelling adds the sixty cities, the iron bed and the praise of God's greatness.

Og is named 'one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei.' The passage lists his territory and confirms that Moses gave it to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh, exactly as Deuteronomy 3:12-17 describes.

Centuries later Solomon's district governor in Ramoth-gilead oversaw 'the region of Argob in Bashan with its sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars.' The detail matches Deuteronomy 3:4-5 and shows how long the memory of Og's fortified kingdom lasted.

Reuben and Gad ask to settle east of the Jordan, Moses warns them with the example of Kadesh, and they pledge to cross armed with their brothers. Deuteronomy 3:18-20 recalls the agreement in brief and keeps the condition in front of the next generation.

The eastern tribes keep the promise of Deuteronomy 3:18-20. Joshua releases them with praise, 'you have not deserted your brothers,' and charges them to love the LORD and hold fast to Him as they return home.

The command of Deuteronomy 3:27 is carried out. Moses climbs Pisgah, the LORD shows him the whole land and says, 'I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it.' Then God Himself buries him opposite Beth-peor, where chapter 3 ends.

Moses is told to view the land and prepare to die, and he responds by asking God to appoint a shepherd for the people. Joshua is commissioned by the laying on of hands. Deuteronomy 3:28 reflects the same concern: Moses' last task is to strengthen his successor.

God speaks to Joshua after Moses' death with the verbs Moses was told to use in Deuteronomy 3:28: 'Be strong and courageous.' The promise that the LORD will fight for Israel, Deuteronomy 3:22, becomes 'I will be with you,' spoken to the new leader.

God reminds Israel that He destroyed the Amorite 'though his height was like that of the cedars.' The prophet appeals to the victories of Deuteronomy 2 and 3 to show Israel's ingratitude, turning the memory of Og into an indictment of those who forgot it.

Moses appears in glory with Elijah, speaking with Jesus about 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.' The man who was not allowed to cross the Jordan stands in the land with Christ, speaking of the greater exodus Christ was about to complete.

Moses was faithful 'as a servant in all God's house,' but Christ is faithful 'as the Son over God's house.' The comparison explains why Moses could lead Israel to the edge of the land but not into it, and why the Son can bring His people all the way.

Paul pleads three times for relief and is told, 'My grace is sufficient for you.' Like Moses in Deuteronomy 3:23-26, a faithful servant hears no to an earnest request, and like Moses he receives in its place a deeper gift of grace and a continuing work.

study.oneStory:
In the story of Scripture, Deuteronomy 3 brings the first stage of the conquest to completion. The promise to Abraham included the defeat of the Amorites whose iniquity had not yet been complete, Genesis 15:16. With Sihon and Og fallen, that judgment has begun, and a portion of the inheritance is already in Israel's hands. The fear that stopped the first generation, the fear of giants, has been answered by the fall of the last king of the Rephaim.

The chapter also answers a question left from Genesis 3: can a human being, even the best of them, bring God's people back into the place of blessing? Moses is the greatest leader Israel ever had, and yet he is barred from the land because of his sin. The pattern of exile from the garden repeats in miniature on the slopes of Pisgah. Only one who is without sin can open the way.

The chapter sets up the rest of Deuteronomy and the book of Joshua. Moses will spend his last days preaching, and then Joshua will lead the people in. The eastern tribes' promise will be kept, the land will be divided, and Israel will enjoy rest. Yet that rest will not last. The eastern tribes will be the first to go into exile, and the whole nation will follow, showing that the land was a shadow of something greater.

The story comes to rest in Christ, the Son who is faithful over God's house, the forerunner who enters ahead of His people, and the victor over powers far greater than Og. In Him Moses himself receives what he was denied, standing in glory in the land and speaking of the exodus Christ would accomplish.

The new creation completes what Pisgah only glimpsed. The faithful of every age, who saw the promises 'from afar,' Hebrews 11:13, will be 'made perfect' together, Hebrews 11:40. God's people will not only see the land; they will inherit a renewed earth, where no enemy remains and no servant of God is left standing on the far side of the river.

quiz.q: What was distinctive about Og's bed, mentioned as evidence of his origin (v.11)?

options.text: It was made of iron, nine cubits long and four cubits wide, a relic of his descent from the Rephaim giants.
options.note: Verse 11 gives this exact detail as proof of Og's remarkable size and ancestry.

options.text: It was made of pure gold.
options.note: The text specifies iron, not gold.

options.text: Nothing distinctive about it is mentioned.
options.note: Verse 11 gives specific, memorable details about it.

options.text: It was the same size as an ordinary bed.
options.note: Its enormous size, nine by four cubits, is exactly the point being made.

quiz.q: What condition did Moses place on the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh for receiving their land east of the Jordan (vv.18-20)?

options.text: Their men of valor had to cross over armed and help their brothers conquer the land west of the Jordan first.
options.note: Verses 18-20 state this condition clearly.

options.text: They had to give up all their livestock.
options.note: Verse 19 explicitly allows their livestock to remain with their families; nothing is confiscated.

options.text: They had to convert their cities into walled fortresses.
options.note: No such building requirement is mentioned here.

options.text: No condition was placed on them at all.
options.note: A clear condition, fighting alongside their brothers first, is stated in verses 18-20.

quiz.q: How did the LORD respond to Moses' plea to cross over into the good land (vv.26-27)?

options.text: He refused, telling Moses to speak no more of it, but let him view the land from Pisgah.
options.note: Verses 26-27 record exactly this firm refusal paired with a real concession.

options.text: He granted the request immediately.
options.note: The text records a clear refusal, not a granted request.

options.text: He postponed the decision indefinitely.
options.note: The refusal in verse 26 is final and immediate, not postponed.

options.text: He gave no response at all.
options.note: Verses 26-27 record a detailed, specific response.

quiz.q: What instruction did Moses give directly to Joshua in this chapter (vv.21-22, 28)?

options.text: Do not be afraid, for the LORD Himself will fight for you; be encouraged and strengthened to lead the people across.
options.note: Verses 21-22 and 28 record this direct commissioning and encouragement.

options.text: Wait several more years before leading the people.
options.note: No delay is instructed; Joshua is commissioned to lead immediately when the time comes.

options.text: Appoint someone else in his place.
options.note: The opposite occurs; Joshua himself is directly commissioned.

options.text: No instruction to Joshua is recorded in this chapter.
options.note: Verses 21-22 and 28 record specific instructions given directly to him.

quiz.q: Why was Moses barred from entering the land, according to his own words here (v.26)?

options.text: The LORD was angry with him on account of the people, and would not listen to his plea.
options.note: Verse 26 states this directly in Moses' own retelling.

options.text: Moses had committed idolatry.
options.note: No such charge is made here or elsewhere against Moses.

options.text: Moses refused to lead the people any further.
options.note: The opposite is true; Moses actively pleaded to continue leading them into the land.

options.text: No reason at all is given here.
options.note: Verse 26 gives a specific, if summarized, reason.

questions: Moses pleaded earnestly with God, yet God said, 'Enough, speak no more of this.' How do you respond when God says no to something you have pleaded for with everything in you?

Even though Moses could not enter the land himself, he poured his remaining strength into commissioning and strengthening Joshua. Who are you investing in and strengthening for a future you may not personally see fulfilled?

The tribes who settled east of the Jordan still had to fight for their brothers before enjoying their own rest. Where is God calling you to serve someone else's need before settling into your own comfort?
Moses was allowed to see the land even though he could not enter it. What are the 'Pisgah views', the partial glimpses of things not yet fully realized, that God has given you?

Og's massive iron bed testified to real, imposing power, yet he still fell before the LORD in a single battle. What imposing obstacle in your life needs to be measured against God's power rather than its own size?

translationNotes.note: The note that Sidonians and Amorites called Mount Hermon by different names, Sirion and Senir, reflects Moses' careful, almost geographer's precision in this historical review.

Og's 'bed of iron' may describe an iron-framed bed or, as some scholars suggest, a black basalt sarcophagus; either reading supports the same point, that Og was an unusually large, formidable figure whose defeat displayed the LORD's power.

'That is enough' translates a short, final Hebrew phrase (rav lakh) that closes off further appeal, showing the LORD's refusal was firm and complete even as He immediately offers Moses a real, if lesser, kindness in verse 27.
